case_name: Mehmet Nuri Özen and Others v. Turkey
court: The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)

facts.text: The applicants are Turkish nationals.

anchor.surface_text: 5.  The applicants are Turkish nationals.

facts.text: They are all serving sentences in Turkish high-security prisons, where the authorities refused to dispatch their letters written in a language other than Turkish.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  They are all serving sentences in Turkish high-security prisons, where the authorities refused to dispatch their letters written in a language other than Turkish.

facts.text: At the time they lodged their applications, the applicants were serving their sentences in the F-type prison in Tekirdağ or the Bolu prison high‑security prison.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  At the time they lodged their applications, the applicants were serving their sentences in the F-type prison in Tekirdağ or the Bolu prison high‑security prison.

facts.text: On 14 January 2008 the Disciplinary Board at the applicant’s prison proceeded, in accordance with section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275, to check a letter the applicant had written to another prisoner in Kurdish and decided to return the letter because they could not have it translated.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 14 January 2008 the Disciplinary Board at the applicant’s prison proceeded, in accordance with section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 on the execution of sentences and preventive measures (“Law no. 5275”), to check a letter the applicant had written to another prisoner in Kurdish. After reminding him that letters should in principle be written in Turkish, they informed him that they could not have the letter translated, for lack of staff, so they were unable to ascertain, as required under Rule 122 § 1 of the Regulations on prison management and the execution of sentences (“the Prison Regulations”), whether the content of the letter was “inoffensive”. They therefore decided to return the letter to the applicant.

facts.text: On 28 January 2008, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decision to return his letter.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 28 January 2008, on the basis of the case file, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal against that decision.

facts.text: On 12 February 2008 the Bolu Assize Court dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant against the enforcements judge's decision.

facts.text: On 21 and 26 September 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to keep one letter written by each of the applicants in Kurdish, requiring translation at applicants' expense before sending.

facts.text: On 6 November 2007, the Tekirdağ enforcements judge dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicants against the decision to withhold letters pending translation at their expense.

Several of them also complained that the national authorities had lacked independence and impartiality, that the disciplinary proceedings had not been public, and that the national courts had failed to give reasons for their decisions (Article 6 § 1). Some also alleged that the proceedings had been unfair (Article 6 § 3 (a), (b) and (c)) and that they had not had access to an effective remedy (Article 13). Lastly, certain applicants relied on Articles 9, 10, 17 and 18 of the Convention.

In their submission the interference with their rights was therefore arbitrary as there was no legal basis for it.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that supervision of correspondence could not justify prohibiting prisoners from corresponding in a language other than Turkish, especially as oral communication in Kurdish was allowed, indicating no legitimate aim was pursued by the ban.

anchor.surface_text: In addition, while the applicants acknowledged that some supervision of correspondence was necessary to guarantee security in prison and prevent crime, they argued that this could not justify prohibiting prisoners from corresponding with their families in a language other than Turkish. In their submission this ban on written communication was in contradiction with the practice of authorising oral communication in another language. There were laws which authorised prisoners to speak Kurdish on the telephone or when they had visitors. This surely indicated that the interference with their correspondence pursued no legitimate aim for the purposes of Article 8 § 2 of the Convention, as the right to speak Kurdish was already acknowledged in prisons.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the refusal to send letters amounted to an interference with the applicants' right to respect for their correspondence under Article 8, regardless of the content of the letters.

anchor.surface_text:
The Court notes that it is not in dispute that the prison authorities refused to forward the applicants’ letters to their addressees, and that the courts concerned upheld those decisions (see paragraphs 8-29 above).

The Court has already held that the mere monitoring of prisoners’ correspondence by the authorities amounts to an “interference” with their right to respect for their correspondence within the meaning of Article 8 (see, for example, Calogero Diana v. Italy, 15 November 1996, § 28, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V). This means that the actual content of the correspondence is immaterial in determining whether a restrictive measure constitutes an “interference”: what counts is whether the private correspondence was interfered with (see Frerot v. France, no. 70204/01, 12 June 2007, § 54).

Clearly, therefore, the decisions not to send the letters amounted to an interference.

arguments.claim: The Court concluded that the interference was not "in accordance with the law" because the refusal to send letters was not based on any legal grounds but on the authorities' inability to understand the letters.

anchor.surface_text: The Court accordingly concludes that the interference complained of was not “in accordance with the law”.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no legal basis for the interference as required by Article 8.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered the circular irrelevant to the period of the violations.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention;
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the refusal to dispatch letters written in a language other than Turkish was an interference with the applicants' correspondence rights under Article 8, that this interference was not "in accordance with the law" as it was based on inability to understand rather than legal grounds, and that the practice of requiring prisoners to pay for translation excluded an entire category of correspondence, thus violating Article 8.
